title: Asia completed TPP without America returning or China taking over
dek: The US extends its China security competition across all Asia policy; China has learned US-style economic coercion; the result is regional fragmentation rather than bipolarity.
why: A theory-strong keynote with rigorous mechanistic argument—TPP as counterexample, Quad's shift from function to form—yet leans on macro narrative; more cases than data.
who: Policy researchers tracking Asia-Pacific geostrategic shifts, middle-power diplomatic space, and US-China competition; corporate heads of global strategy.
skip: The host's lengthy opening remarks and chitchat (0:14-6:23) can be skipped without losing the argument.

points.h: Asia completed TPP without America returning or China taking over
points.body: Obama defended TPP saying ‘we don't write the rules, China will’. After Trump withdrew, the other 11 members completed the deal—neither America returned nor China joined. This shows how regional order actually works: not through binary US-China competition, but through first movers—countries like Chile, New Zealand, Singapore, Brunei that liberalize first and set the template for others to join.

points.h: US and China are the same: both strategic narcissists fixated on each other
points.body: US and China have almost nothing in common—different political systems, economic models, strategic logic—yet share one striking quality: both treat nearly all regional affairs as expressions of their mutual competition. Evan calls this ‘strategic narcissism’. He acknowledges this contradicts the Chinese position on Belt and Road as win-win cooperation, but judges that China is learning American behavior. The two countries' patterns are converging.

points.h: America's focus on China security has absorbed its entire Asia strategy
points.body: The US securitizes China policy: nearly all economic flows—goods, capital, people, technology, data—now pass through a national-security filter. Simultaneously, it China-izes Asia policy: China becomes the sole reference point for almost every regional decision. The result: the entire Asia policy itself becomes securitized. Regional countries have begun asking what else America actually offers.

points.h: US-Korea and US-Australia alliances shifting from local defense to Taiwan
points.body: US-Korea alliance once focused almost exclusively on North Korea; Taiwan is now unavoidable. US-Australia ties, structured since the 1952 Radford-Collins agreement around geographic division of labor, now have America pushing Australia to extend strategy into Taiwan contingencies, expand forward positioning, adjust logistics, and raise defense spending to 3.5% of GDP.

points.h: America wants hegemony without paying the cost of public goods
points.body: Evan finds America's regional policy ‘strong on attitude, weak on strategy; strong on security, weak on everything else’. It has no coherent regional vision (no longer pushing trade liberalization) and no consistent logic (why antagonize all allies if the goal is balancing China?—yet China-focused competition has led the US to trade wars with India, not China). America is pursuing ‘empire on the cheap’: maintaining hegemony while closing markets and withdrawing public goods.

points.h: China is adopting America's toolkit of economic coercion
points.body: China's Central Asian economic ties have shifted from oil and gas to digital infrastructure and renewables, giving China gravitational pull through geography and economy, without needing to ‘persuade’. But China is also copying American coercion methods. America has the Entity List; China created the unreliable entities list. America sanctions firms and people; so does China. More absurd: Hong Kong's National Security Law Article 29, Section 4 makes compliance with foreign sanctions illegal—China has written extraterritorial jurisdiction into its own statute.

points.h: Solve functional problems with real coalitions, not ceremonial forums
points.body: US officials have recently obsessed with building trilateral and quadrilateral mechanisms; someone seriously proposed the US-Japan-Kazakhstan arrangement. Evan's counter: what's the point? His advice to middle powers: stop chasing form. Instead, assemble genuinely capable countries to solve concrete functional problems. DEPA, the digital trade agreement, emerged when four TPP countries collaborated; that's how rules get set in a world where both America and China are faltering.

points.h: Quad worked for nine days, then became purely symbolic diplomacy
points.body: Quad started in 2004 as a tsunami-relief mechanism. In nine days, the US, Japan, Australia, and India finished the rescue. No ministerial meetings. No summit. No joint communiqué. No secretariat. Task done—the mechanism dissolved itself. When Japan later revived Quad, the emphasis shifted to form: summits, photo opportunities, declarations. Evan criticizes this: people now debate whether Quad works precisely because it became formal machinery rather than functional response.
